procedural_history.impugned_order: Order and decision of the learned Special Judge Shri R.B.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Criminal revision application could have been heard under Sec. 407 Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and transferred the Special case from which criminal revision application arose to itself for trial.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Criminal Appeal No. 356 of 1983 and Criminal Misc. Petition No. 1740 of 1984 were filed in the Supreme Court. The appeal was allowed.

directions: The order and decision of the learned Special Judge Shri R.B. Sule dated July 25, 1983 discharging the accused in Special Case No. 24 of 1982 and Special Case No. 3/83 is hereby set aside.
The trial shall proceed further from the stage where the accused was discharged.

issue.issue_text: Whether the order of the Special Judge discharging the accused in Special Case No. 24 of 1982 and Special Case No. 3/83 was legally correct and sustainable.

facts: The Special Judge, Shri R.B. Sule, issued an order on July 25, 1983, discharging the accused in Special Case No. 24 of 1982 and Special Case No. 3/83.
This discharge order was challenged through a Criminal Revision Application, which was heard by the Supreme Court as part of a larger appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 356 of 1983).
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the Special Judge's order discharging the accused.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court explicitly set aside the Special Judge's order of July 25, 1983. By doing so, it rejected the legality of the discharge and ordered that the trial must proceed from the stage where the accused had been discharged.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the order of the Special Judge discharging the accused in Special Case No. 24 of 1982 and Special Case No. 3/83 was legally correct and sustainable.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (complainant) sought clarification that the advocate they engaged should be deemed the public prosecutor for the trial.

Under Section 8(3) of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1952, if cognizance is taken under Section 8(1), the advocate engaged by the complainant to conduct the prosecution is deemed to be a public prosecutor.
It is the complainant's right to decide who will be the advocate in charge of the prosecution, and there is no requirement to entrust the trial to a State-appointed public prosecutor.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (accused) argued that the petition for clarification was a 'covert attempt to forestall or foreclose the decision' on procedural issues that were pending before the trial judge.

cases.principle: For the interpretation of Sec. 5(1) and Sec. 8(3) of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1952, establishing that an advocate engaged by the complainant to conduct the prosecution is deemed to be a public prosecutor.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When cognizance of an offense is taken under Section 8(1) of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1952, the trial must follow the procedure for warrant cases instituted otherwise than on a police report as prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure. In such a trial, the advocate engaged by the complainant is deemed to be a public prosecutor, and it is for the complainant to decide who will be in charge of the prosecution.
obiter: If the judgment of this Court was read with care and precision, these two questions would have hardly arisen.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that based on a plain reading of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1952, if cognizance of an offense is taken under Section 8(1), then Section 8(3) automatically applies. This means the advocate engaged by the complainant to conduct the prosecution is, by law, deemed to be a public prosecutor. Consequently, it is the complainant's right to decide who will be the advocate in charge of the prosecution, and there is no requirement or question of entrusting the trial to a State-appointed public prosecutor.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 8(3) of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1952, if cognizance of an offence is taken under Section 8(1) of that Act, the advocate engaged by the complainant to conduct the prosecution will be deemed to be a public prosecutor.

Under Section 407(8) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, when a case is transferred to a High Court for trial, the High Court must follow the same procedure that the original court (in this case, the Court of Special Judge) would have followed.

The procedure to be followed for the trial is that prescribed in Chapter XIX-B (Sections 244 to 247) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which governs cases instituted otherwise than on a police report.
policy_considerations: The court issued the clarification on the procedural matters in order to 'thwart avoidable delay in the trial of cases'.
